fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says, "Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them." (Ezekiel 6:2) Son of man is what God calls Ezekiel here. So Ezekiel gets his orders: turn and face the mountains, and speak. Not the easiest audience to preach to, but a prophet goes where he's sent.

Nineveh isn't in this message. God tells Ezekiel to set his face against "…the mountains of Israel…" (Ezekiel 6:2). Ezekiel isn't pointed at walls at all, but at mountains, which is odd enough that it sticks with you. Nice guess on the walls, though.

Babylon is a name that might come to mind, so I see why you picked it. But God doesn't point Ezekiel at any gates. He says, "Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them." (Ezekiel 6:2) The message is for the mountains of Israel.

Yes, friend! God says, "I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places." (Ezekiel 6:3) He says it again in verse 6: the high places will be demolished. So the high places are right in the middle of this message.

Palaces make sense if you're picturing a sword aimed at kings, but that's not what God says here. He says, "I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places." (Ezekiel 6:3) Verse 6 repeats that the high places will be demolished. No palaces in this verse at all.

That's it. God says, "…I will cast down your slain before your idols." (Ezekiel 6:4) Verse 5 says it again: He will lay the corpses of the Israelites before their idols. Right in front of the idols. It's a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly: this one hurts.

Not quite, friend. God says the opposite: "Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste…" (Ezekiel 6:6) So the cities aren't spared. The same verse says the high places will be demolished and the altars laid waste and desecrated.

Right, baker. The statement is false because God says, "Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste…" (Ezekiel 6:6) So the cities aren't spared. The high places, altars, idols and incense altars are all named in that same verse. It's a long list, and the cities are on it.

Making excuses is a very human move, I've done it with burnt batches. But that's not what the verse says. It says, "So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations." (Ezekiel 6:9) Loathing is what the survivors do.

That's the one. God says, "Clap your hands, stomp your feet…" (Ezekiel 6:11) He also tells Ezekiel to cry out "Alas!" over the abominations of the house of Israel. So Ezekiel gets a whole-body assignment. No sitting still for this prophet.

Tearing a robe and sitting in ashes do show up in the Bible, like Job tearing his robe (Job 1:20) and sitting among the ashes (Job 2:8). But that's not what God asks of Ezekiel here. He says, "Clap your hands, stomp your feet…" (Ezekiel 6:11) So it's clapping and stomping, not ashes. I'd say that's a pretty loud assignment.

Ezekiel does get an assignment like that earlier, when he's told to lie on his side (Ezekiel 4:4–6), so I see where it came from. But in this verse, God says, "Clap your hands, stomp your feet…" (Ezekiel 6:11) It's hands and feet and a shout, not lying down.

Hiding in the hills sounds sensible, but that isn't what the verse says. It calls them "…the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols." (Ezekiel 6:13) So the verse names them as places where incense was offered to idols. The slain will lie among their idols there.

Homes would be a nice thought, but the verse has something else in mind. It calls them "…the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols." (Ezekiel 6:13) The high hills and leafy oaks are named as places where they offered incense. The slain will lie among their idols there.
